'''''Nymphoides peltata''''', the '''fringed water-lily'''<ref name="PlantAtlas">{{cite web |title=Fringed Water-lily ''Nymphoides peltata'' Kuntze |website=PlantAtlas |url=https://plantatlas2020.org/atlas/2cd4p9h.vp2 |access-date=5 September 2025}}</ref> is perennial, rooted aquatic plant with floating leaves of the family [[Menyanthaceae]]. Synonyms include ''Menyanthes nymphoides'' L., ''Villarsia nymphoides'', ''Limnanthemum peltatum'' S.G.Gmel., ''Nymphoides nymphoides'' (L.) Britton, and other vernacular names include yellow floating heart, floating heart, water fringe, and entire marshwort.

It is native throughout most of Europe (excluding Ireland and Scandinavia) and temperate Asia, and locally in Algeria in northwest Africa.<ref name="POWO">{{cite web |title=Nymphoides peltata (S.G.Gmel.) Kuntze |website=Plants of the World Online |date=17 July 2020 |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:370207-1 |access-date=5 September 2025}}</ref>

It has been spread by human cultivation outside its native range and is now [[naturalisation (biology)|naturalised]] in Ireland,<ref name="PlantAtlas"/> Denmark and Sweden,<ref name="POWO"/> much of North America,<ref name="POWO"/><ref name="USGS">{{cite web |title=Nymphoides peltata (S.G. Gmel.) Kuntze |url=https://nas.er.usgs.gov/queries/FactSheet.aspx?speciesID=243 |website=USGS |access-date=24 March 2018}}</ref><ref name="Nault">{{cite web |last1=Nault |first1=Michelle E. |last2=Mikulyuk |first2=Allison |title=Yellow Floating Heart (Nymphoides peltata): A Technical Review of Distribution, Ecology, Impacts, and Management |url=https://dnr.wi.gov/files/PDF/pubs/ss/SS1051.pdf |website=Wisconsin DNR |access-date=24 March 2018}}</ref> and New Zealand.<ref name="Nault" /> In many of its introduced regions, ''N. peltata'' is considered a noxious weed because it can form dense mats that shade out locally native aquatic plant species, thereby reducing biodiversity.<ref name="Nault" />

==Description==
[[File:Nymphoides peltata kz29.jpg|thumb|left|Leaves, Odra valley near Bielinek, Poland]]
[[File:Nymphoides peltata on cracked mud, Appledore (52260634916).jpg|thumb|''Nymphoides peltata'' during a drought, at Appledore, Devon, England]]
Fringed water-lily is an aquatic, bottom-rooted perennial species with underwater creeping [[stolons]] that extend in water up to 2 metres deep.<ref name="PlantAtlas" /><ref name="Streeter">{{cite book |last=Streeter |first=David |title=Flower Guide |publisher=Collins |publication-place=London |date=2010 |isbn=978-0-00-718389-0 |page=370}}</ref><ref name="Blamey">{{cite book |last1=Blamey |first1=Marjorie |last2=Grey-Wilson |first2=Christopher |title=The Illustrated Flora of Britain and Northern Europe |publisher=Hodder & Stoughton |publication-place=London [ |date=1 January 1989 |isbn=0-340-40170-2 |page=310}}</ref> Each [[Plant stem|node]] on a stolon can produce a new shoot and roots.<ref name="GISD">{{cite web |title=Nymphoides peltata |url=http://www.iucngisd.org/gisd/species.php?sc=225 |website=The Global Invasive Species Database |access-date=24 March 2018}}</ref> ''N. peltata'' has [[Cordate (leaf shape)|cordate]] floating leaves that are 3–12 cm (rarely to 15 cm) diameter, nearly circular but with wavy margins and a narrow slit extending to the stem; they are green to yellow-green, often with purple blotches above and purple undersides, and are attach to submerged [[rhizomes]].<ref name="Blamey"/><ref name="Streeter"/> The leaves have slightly wavy margins and support a lax, or loose, [[inflorescence]] of two to five yellow flowers 3–4 cm diameter with a five-lobed corolla, and fringed petal margins.<ref name="Streeter"/><ref name="Michigan">{{cite web |title=Nymphoides peltata (S.G.Gmel.) Kuntze |url=http://michiganflora.net/species.aspx?id=2922 |website=University of Michigan Herbarium |access-date=22 November 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161122225056/http://michiganflora.net/species.aspx?id=2922 |archive-date=22 November 2016}}</ref> ''N. peltata'' flower [[peduncle (botany)|peduncle]]s rise a short distance out of the water.<ref name="Blamey" /> Each flower produces a 1.5–2.5 cm beaked capsule which hold many flattened seeds with stiff marginal hairs.<ref name="Michigan" /><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Sivarajan |first1=V. V . |last2=Joseph |first2=K. T. |title=The genus Nymphoides Seguier (Menyanthaceae) in India |journal=Aquatic Botany |date=1993 |volume=45 |issue=2–3 |pages=145–170 |doi=10.1016/0304-3770(93)90019-s |bibcode=1993AqBot..45..145S }}</ref>

[[File:2018.09.25.-02-Grand Etang de Birieux-Birieux--Europaeische Seekanne.jpg|thumb|left|The frilled fringes on the flower margin which give the species its English name. Grand Étang de Birieux, near Lyon, France.]]
''N. peltata'' is similar in appearance to species in the genera ''[[Nuphar]]'' and ''[[Nymphaea]]'' in the family [[Nymphaeaceae]]. It can be distinguished from both by its wavy-margined leaf, and by the flowers being in clusters of 2–5 together rather than singly.<ref name="Streeter"/> ''Nuphar'' can also be distinguished from ''N. peltata'' most easily by its larger leaves, which can measure up to 30 cm, and its cup-shaped flower.<ref name="Streeter"/> ''Nymphaea'' have angled leaf bases as opposed to the rounded leaf bases of ''Nymphoides'', and ''Nymphoides'' have significantly longer peduncles that support smaller flowers.<ref name="Nault" /> In order to identify different species within ''Nymphoides'', flowers are usually required.<ref name="Nault" />

==Ecology==
[[File:Nymphoides peltata sl18.jpg|thumb|Immature fruit, at Gmünd, Austria]]
''N. peltata'' is a freshwater species and does not occur in waters with an average [[salinity]] exceeding about 300 mg/L.<ref name="Van der Velder">{{cite journal |last1=Van der Velder |first1=G. |last2=Giesen |first2=T. G. |last3=Van der Heijden |first3=L. |title=Structure, biomass and seasonal changes in biomass of Nymphoides peltata (Gmel.) O. Kuntze (Menyanthaceae), a preliminary study |journal=Aquatic Botany |date=1979 |volume=7 |pages=279–399 |doi=10.1016/0304-3770(79)90029-9 |bibcode=1979AqBot...7..279V }}</ref> ''N. peltata'' is most commonly found in slow-moving rivers, lakes, ponds, and reservoirs, but it can also establish in swamps and wetlands.<ref name="Nault" /> It is also known to occur in ditches, canals, break-through pools of dikes, and backwaters, especially those subject to winter flooding.<ref name="Van der Velder" /><ref name="Van der Voo">{{cite journal |last1=Van der Voo |first1=E. E. |last2=Westhoff |first2=V. |title=An autecological study of some limnophytes and helophytes in the area of the large rivers |journal=Wentia |date=1961 |volume=5 |issue=163–258 |page=163 |doi=10.1111/j.1438-8677.1961.tb00008.x |bibcode=1961Wenti...5..163V }}</ref> The presence of N. peltata can signal an environment with water movement.<ref name="Van der Velder" />

Depending on water temperature, ''N. peltata'' flowers mainly between July and September,<ref name="Blamey"/> with outside dates from May to October.<ref name="Nault" /> Each flower survives a single day, while leaves can persist from 23–43 days.<ref name="Nault" /> Seeds are released 32–60 days following the end of the flowering period and can germinate under [[Hypoxia (environmental)|hypoxic]] conditions.<ref name="Smits">{{cite journal |last1=Smits |first1=A. J. M. |last2=Van Avesaath |first2=P. H. |last3=Van der Velde |first3=G. |title=Germination requirements and seed banks of some nymphaeid macrophytes: ''Nymphaea alba'' L., ''Nuphar lutea'' (L.) Sm. and ''Nymphoides peltata'' (Gmel.) O. Kuntze |journal=Freshwater Biology |date=1990 |volume=24 |issue=2 |pages=315–326 |doi=10.1111/j.1365-2427.1990.tb00712.x |bibcode=1990FrBio..24..315S }}</ref><ref name="Van der Velde 1981">{{cite journal |last1=Van der Velde |first1=G. |last2=Van der Heijden |first2=L. A. |title=The floral biology and seed production of Nymphoides peltata (Gmel.) O. Kuntze (Menyanthaceae) |journal=Aquatic Botany |date=1981 |volume=10 |pages=261–293 |doi=10.1016/0304-3770(81)90027-9 |bibcode=1981AqBot..10..261V }}</ref> In fall, the aboveground biomass of ''N. peltata'' dies, sinks to the substrate and decomposes, and the plant overwinters as dormant rhizomes.<ref name="USGS" /> These rhizomes can survive freezing temperatures down to −30 °C.<ref name="Darbyshire" /> During the winter, stolons and stems either on or buried beneath the substrate can remain dormant until spring, and some small submerged leaves measuring 1–2 cm sometimes grow on these stems.<ref name="Darbyshire" /> After winter, the species requires light and oxygen to produce new growth and floating leaves begin to appear in spring.<ref name="Smits" />

''N. peltata'' can reproduce vegetatively or sexually. Fragments of one plant, including [[stolons]], [[rhizomes]], and leaves attached to part of a stem, can also develop into a new plant.<ref name="Nault" /> Seeds are produced either by cross or self-pollination, though self-pollination usually produces fewer and less viable seeds than cross-pollination.<ref name="Ornduff">{{cite journal |last1=Ornduff |first1=R. |title=The origin of dioecism from heterostyly in Nymphoides (Menyanthaceae) |journal=Evolution |date=1996 |volume=20 |issue=3 |pages=309–314 |pmid=28562972 |doi=10.1111/j.1558-5646.1966.tb03368.x |s2cid=40969352}}</ref> Seed dispersal is facilitated by the semi-hydrophobia of seeds, which causes them to float on the water's surface until disturbed.<ref name="Cook" /> Seeds are suited to adhering to surfaces such as the flanks, folds of skin on digit webs, and the short feathers on the heads of waterfowl, which are [[hydrophobic]].<ref name ="Cook">{{cite journal |last1=Cook |first1=C. D. K. |title=Seed dispersal of Nymphoides peltata (S.G. Gmelin) O. Kuntze (Menyanthaceae) |journal=Aquatic Botany |date=1990 |volume=37 |issue=4 |pages=325–340 |doi=10.1016/0304-3770(90)90019-h |bibcode=1990AqBot..37..325C }}</ref> While in flight, the marginal [[trichomes]] surround the seeds keep the seeds attached to the bird, but once again in water, the seeds detach and sink to the substrate, where germination can commence.<ref name ="Cook" /> Adherence to amphibious animals and boats are two other possible dispersal mechanisms.<ref name="Darbyshire" /> Conversely, seeds that are eaten by waterfowl or fish are completely digested and no longer viable.<ref name="Smits 1989">{{cite journal |last1=Smits |first1=A. J. M. |last2=Van Ruremonde |first2=R. |last3=Van der Velde |first3=G. |title=Seed dispersal of three nymphaeid macrophytes |journal=Aquatic Botany |date=1989 |volume=35 |issue=2 |pages=167–180 |doi=10.1016/0304-3770(89)90103-4 |bibcode=1989AqBot..35..167S }}</ref>

''N. peltata'' is critically endangered in Spain, Belarus, and the Czech Republic, endangered in Lithuania, and vulnerable in Germany, Switzerland and Japan.<ref name="iucn status 12 November 2021" />

==As an invasive species==
''N. peltata'' are commonly sold for use in ornamental water gardens.<ref name="Nault" /><ref name="Darbyshire" /> The species is intentionally or accidentally transferred to lakes and rivers outside of its native range.<ref name="USGS" /> In the United States, the first recorded occurrence of the plant was in 1882 in Massachusetts,<ref name="Nault" /> and the plant has been sold domestically since the 1930s.<ref name="USDA">{{cite web |title=Weed Risk Assessment for Nymphoides peltata (S. G. Gmel.) Kuntze (Menyanthaceae) – Yellow floating heart |url=https://plants.ifas.ufl.edu/wp-content/uploads/files/caip/pdfs/USDA-APHIS-WRA%20Nymphoides%20peltata-2012.pdf |website=U.S. Department of Agriculture |access-date=25 March 2018}}</ref> ''N. peltata'' has been recorded in 29 U.S. states and Washington, D.C., and it has naturalised in slow-moving waters.<ref name="USGS" /><ref name="Darbyshire" /> In Canada, ''N. peltata'' has been found in [[Newfoundland]], Nova Scotia, Quebec, Ontario, and British Columbia, but has not yet been naturalised.<ref name="Darbyshire" /> ''N. peltata'' was intentionally introduced to Sweden in the early 19th century and was first recorded as a non-indigenous species in 1870.[2] Native to central and eastern [[Great Britain|Britain]], ''N. peltata'' was transported northern Britain and Ireland as an ornamental plant<ref name="Kelly">{{cite web |last1=Kelly |first1=J. |last2=Maguire |first2=C. M. |title=Fringed Water Lily (Nymphoides peltata) Invasive Species Action Plan |url=https://invasivespeciesireland.com/wp-content/uploads/2010/11/Nymphoides_peltata_ISAP.pdf |website=Invasive Species Ireland |access-date=25 March 2018 |archive-date=27 October 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191027103320/https://invasivespeciesireland.com/wp-content/uploads/2010/11/Nymphoides_peltata_ISAP.pdf}}</ref> and first documented in Ireland in before 1866.<ref name="Nault" /> In 1988, ''N. peltata'' was discovered in New Zealand, where it is considered a [[noxious weed]].<ref name="Nault" /> It is also designated an invasive species in Sweden, Ireland, and parts of North America.<ref name="Nault" />

''N. peltata'' spreads the most aggressively in [[Trophic state index#Eutrophic|eutrophic lakes]] with neutral to [[alkaline]] water, but the species has also been found in [[Trophic state index#Oligotrophic|oligotrophic lakes]] and [[acidic]] ponds.<ref name="Darbyshire">{{cite journal |last1=Darbyshire |first1=S. J. |last2=Francis |first2=A. |title=The Biology of Invasive Alien Plants in Canada. 10. Nymphoides peltata (S. G. Gmel.) Kuntze |journal=Canadian Journal of Plant Science |date=2008 |volume=88 |issue=4 |pages=811–829 |doi=10.4141/cjps07208 |doi-access=free}}</ref> It most frequently occurs in water 1 to 1.5 m deep, but it can survive in water between 0.3 and 3.0 metres deep.<ref name="Van der Velder" /> The ideal substrate for ''N. peltata'' consists of clay or clay covered with a thin layer of [[sapropel]].<ref name="Darbyshire" /> ''N. peltata'' occurs in temperate environments and has even been found eastern Ontario and western Russia.<ref name="Darbyshire" /> The northernmost limit of ''N. peltata'' is approximately the 16 °C July [[isotherm (contour line)|isotherm]].<ref name="Van der Voo" />

''N. peltata'' can have many negative ecological and social impacts on its introduced regions. ''N. peltata'' can rapidly grow and spread to form dense patches of vegetation on the water's surface that restrict the amount of light penetrating the surface.<ref name="USGS" /> As a result, native submerged macrophytes are excluded and [[biodiversity]] is reduced.<ref name="USDA" /> Especially if algae are shaded out, entire food webs can be disrupted by dense populations of ''N. peltata''.<ref name="Kelly" /> Dense ''N. peltata'' mats can also reduce the amount of oxygen in water and create stagnant water areas.<ref name="USGS" /> Fish and other aquatic wildlife can also be forced to relocate once ''N. peltata'' mats form.<ref name="USDA" /> ''N. peltata'' also affects internal fertilisation patterns as it moves nitrogen and phosphorus up from the sediment to its floating biomass as it grows and releases these nutrients back into the ecosystem during its winter decomposition.<ref name="Darbyshire" />

===Control strategies===
As ''N. peltata'' can propagate through fragmentation, mechanical control is a challenging strategy because it can often aid in dispersal. One approach is to cut leaf petioles one to two times each spring and summer.<ref name="DiTomaso">{{cite web |last1=DiTomaso |first1=J. M. |last2=Kyser |first2=G. B. |title=Weed Control in Natural Areas in the Western United States: Yellow floatingheart |url=http://wric.ucdavis.edu/information/natural%20areas/wr_N/Nymphoides.pdf |publisher=Weed Research and Information Center, University of California |access-date=24 March 2018}}</ref> Cutting, harvesting, and covering plants with barrier materials can sometimes result in a successful control effort.<ref name="DiTomaso" /> Hand raking can be a viable strategy in very localised areas.<ref name="Nault" /> However, [[dredging]] is not an effective method as roots and rhizomes can survive mechanical dredging.<ref name="DiTomaso" />

There are no known effective biological control agents for ''N. peltata''. While [[grass carp]] may feed on parts of ''N. peltata'', the fish usually first consumes submerged macrophytes and has not been shown to feed on ''N. peltata''.<ref name="DiTomaso" />

[[Glyphosate]] applied to floating leaves after emergence during late spring or summer has been used as a chemical control for ''N. peltata''.<ref name="DiTomaso" /> Nonetheless, repeated applications are necessary,<ref name="DiTomaso" /> and spraying floating leaves shows 40-50% control for a single season.<ref name="Nault" /> [[Dichlobenil]] is more effective than glyphosate in controlling ''N. peltata''.<ref name="Nault" /> The application of the chemical in the spring during emergence coupled with mechanical removal of floating leaves and repeated dichlobenil applications has been successful.<ref name="Nault" /> However, the producers of dichlobenil advise not to treat more than 20% of a waterbody and to not treat areas where flow exceeds 90m/hour.<ref name="Nault" /> In Ireland, dichlobenil is no longer legally allowed to be used near or in waterbodies as it can potentially harm other aquatic organisms such as fish.<ref name="Kelly" />

==Uses==
''N. peltata'' is an [[edible plant]]. Leaves and flowers are cooked as a [[potherb]], and so are the stems, but only the interior of the stem is eaten.<ref name="Lim">{{cite book |last1=Lim |first1=T. K. |title=Edible Medicinal and Non Medicinal Plants: Volume 8, Flowers |date=2014 |publisher=Springer}}</ref> Seeds are ground and used for other culinary purposes.<ref name="Lim" /> The fresh leaves are commonly used to treat headaches.{{Citation needed|date=May 2021}}
